title: Jacky Kwok @ COLM 2026 (@jackyk02) — thread (11 tweets)
summary:
[1/11] ✨ Test-Time Scaling for Robotics ✨
Excited to release 🤖 RoboMonkey, which characterizes test-time scaling laws for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and introduces a framework that significantly improves the generalization and robustness of VLAs!
🧵(1 / N)
🌐 Website:
💻 Code:
🗂️ Datasets and Models:
🚀 Serving Engine:
📄 Paper:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gvb4E7WWQAE1TgA.jpg
────────
[2/11] 🧵(2 / N) Test-time scaling law for VLAs:
We observe that action error consistently decreases 📉 as we scale the number of generated actions. Repeatedly sampling actions from robot policies, applying Gaussian perturbation to a few sampled actions, and even random sampling of discrete action tokens all outperform single-attempt OpenVLA, assuming the presence of an oracle verifier. We also find that the relationship between action error and the number of samples generated through Gaussian Perturbation follows an approximate power law across a range of VLA models, including CogACT, Octo, OpenVLA, and SpatialVLA.
────────
[3/11] 🧵(3 / N) Core Questions:
- 1️⃣ Can we capitalize on these scaling laws with a learned action verifier to improve policy robustness?
- 2️⃣ Can we scale synthetic data to improve verification and downstream tasks?
- 3️⃣ How do we enable practical deployment for test-time scaling?
────────
[4/11] 🧵(4 / N) Training:
Given a robotics dataset, we sample N actions per state from a policy. We construct synthetic action preferences based on the RMSE between each sampled action and the ground-truth action. This dataset is then used to fine-tune a VLM-based action verifier.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GvcWAsGWkAAWVY0.jpg
────────
[5/11] 🧵(5 / N) Scaling:
At deployment, we sample a small batch of actions from a policy. We use Gaussian perturbation and majority voting to efficiently generate more action candidates based on the initial samples. Finally, the VLM-based verifier is used to select the optimal action.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GvcWGYbXYAEccs_.jpg
────────
[6/11] 🧵(6 / N) Eval:
We show that pairing existing VLAs with RoboMonkey yields significant performance gains 🦾 achieving a 25% absolute improvement on real-world out-of-distribution tasks, 9% on in-distribution SIMPLER environments, and 7% on LIBERO-Long benchmark.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GvcWLHOX0AA8jAi.jpg
────────
[7/11] 🧵(7 / N) We find that RoboMonkey effectively mitigates issues of imprecise grasping, task progression failures, and collisions at deployment. Detailed task breakdowns and failure analysis are provided on our project website:
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/GvcWTgKXsAABwM6.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/tweet_video/GvcWTgKXsAABwM6.mp4
────────
[8/11] 🧵(8 / N) Scaling the synthetic dataset size (number of action comparisons) 📈 consistently improves the performance of the RoboMonkey verifier, leading to higher closed-loop success rates on SIMPLER.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GvcWiSHWUAAHQiR.jpg
────────
[9/11] 🧵(9 / N) To enable practical deployment for test-time scaling, we implemented a VLA serving engine on top of SGLang to speed up 🚀 repeated sampling of initial action candidates and employ Gaussian perturbation to efficiently construct an action proposal distribution.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GvcWnh6XYAAmVc9.jpg
────────
[10/11] 📋 Takeaways
Rather than framing robot control as a generation problem, we suggest that viewing it through the lens of sampling and verification—generating diverse action candidates and verifying them—can be an effective path towards general-purpose robotics foundation models.
────────
[11/11] This work was an awesome collaboration between Stanford, UC Berkeley, and NVIDIA. It was made possible by an incredible team: @agiachris @RohanSinhaSU @MatthewFoutter @depetrol1 and amazing advisors: @drmapavone @Azaliamirh @istoica05

title: Jacky Kwok @ COLM 2026 (@jackyk02) — thread (14 tweets)
summary:
[1/14] How can we extract richer signals from AI Feedback?
Introducing LLM-as-a-Verifier✨— a simple verification scaling framework that achieves SOTA on agentic benchmarks 🚀
The key idea:
- Use fine-grained scoring granularity (e.g., 1-20 instead of the standard 1-5 scale)
- Take the expectation over the full logprob distribution of score tokens
- Scale repeated evaluation and criteria decomposition
You can use these fine-grained signals for more effective test-time scaling, RL, and agent monitoring! It achieves SOTA across Terminal-Bench V2, SWE-Bench Verified, RoboRewardBench, and MedAgentBench 👑
Advised by @Azaliamirh @istoica05 @drmapavone @chelseabfinn
🧵👇
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMvFN6qbMAA6FeR.jpg
────────
[2/14] 🌐 Website:
📄 Paper:
📖 API:
💻 Code:
🛠️ Claude Code Plugin:
🗣️ Slack:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMvGKqSbUAAA0h4.jpg
────────
[3/14] 🧵(1) Test-Time Scaling
LLM-as-a-Verifier achieves SOTA performance on Terminal-Bench V2 (86.5%), SWE-Bench Verified (78.2%), RoboRewardBench (87.4%), and MedAgentBench (73.3%) when used as a trajectory reward model for test-time scaling.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMvGPhTa0AAGHxE.jpg
────────
[4/14] 🧵(2) Reinforcement Learning
LLM-as-a-Verifier can be used as a dense reward signal for RL, improving the sample efficiency of SAC and GRPO on robotics and mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMvGSXFbEAA7t4V.jpg
────────
[5/14] 🧵(3) Progress Tracking — 💻 Coding
We observe a strong correlation between the chronological order of code generation steps and the scores from LLM-as-a-Verifier. The successful trajectory of the pytorch-model-cli task from Terminal-Bench follows a coherent sequence of events—Read → Install g++ compiler → Install CPU-only torch → Update hidden_dim → DONE and exhibits consistently increasing verifier scores. In contrast, the failed trajectory is characterized by erroneous behaviors, resulting in significantly lower scores.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMvGb82aMAAPD_7.jpg
────────
[6/14] 🧵(4) Progress Tracking — 🤖 Robotics
LLM-as-a-Verifier generates a smooth, temporally aligned progress signal over the course of rollout while remaining robust to failure modes such as incorrect intent or imprecise grasping.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2074970296806002688/img/9A_Q7vJvIqALyzB5.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/amplify_video/2074970296806002688/vid/avc1/630x270/CTqW2NEe_ZhX-tCG.mp4?tag=28
────────
[7/14] 🧵(5) APIs
Adapt LLM-as-a-Verifier to your own use case with a simple API:
pip install llm-verifier
API documentation:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMvGpOfbUAAW1JH.png
────────
[8/14] 🧵(6) Motivation
Most agents already "know" how to solve the tasks. On Terminal-Bench, if you repeatedly sample 100 trajectories per task, they can outperform Claude Mythos and nearly solve the entire benchmark. But the problem is that they don’t know which one is correct.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMvGu1WasAAq-df.jpg
────────
[9/14] 🧵(7) Tie Rate
While standard LLM-as-a-Judge can be used here, they fail to provide sufficiently fine-grained feedback. When comparing complex solutions, judges often assign the same score, resulting in a tie. Coarse scoring leads to 27% ties on Terminal-Bench V2.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMvGzi0bsAAUke2.jpg
────────
[10/14] 🧵(8) Case Study
Turns out computing the expectation over the distribution of scoring token logits can break these ties! On query-optimize task, the discrete judge almost always ties, whereas LLM-as-a-Verifier correctly ranks the better trajectory in 77/100 runs with zero ties.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMvG5BxbEAARY2R.jpg
────────
[11/14] 🧵(9) Verification Scaling
This probabilistic formulation enables verification to scale along multiple dimensions. We show that scaling the scoring granularity leads to better separation between positive and negative solutions. Moreover, scaling repeated evaluation and criteria decomposition consistently leads to additional gains in verification accuracy through variance and complexity reduction.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMvG_eEboAAMEvY.jpg
────────
[12/14] 🧵(10) Example Prompt & Fine-Grained Reward Estimation
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMvHBkVasAAsXXi.jpg
────────
[13/14] 🧵(11) Ranking Algorithm
We also introduce a cost-efficient algorithm for selecting the best solution among candidates using the preference probabilities derived from the verifier. It reduces the complexity from O(N²) to O(Nk), where k denotes a small set of pivot candidates.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMvHGdka0AArqNz.jpg
────────
[14/14] Want to apply LLM-as-a-Verifier to your own tasks?
1️⃣ To verify almost anything, use our API:
2️⃣ For daily vibe coding, try TurboAgent:
3️⃣ To adapt it to existing agent trajectories, modify a simple prompt template:
We’d love feedback, contributions, and new use cases from the community!

title: Jacky Kwok @ COLM 2026 (@jackyk02) — thread (14 tweets)
clean_title: Contrastive Language Model (CLM) for fast multimodal action verification
summary:
[1/14] CLM-8B is part of our scaling ladder, where we train models across multiple scales to establish scaling laws and predict performance at larger scales. A multimodal CLM-35B is now in training with more data, compute, and parameters. Stay tuned for the release early next month 🚀
────────
[2/14] Joint work with @hangoo_kang @TarunSures41845 @JonSaadFalcon @drmapavone @Azaliamirh and @HazyResearch
────────
[3/14] @hangoo_kang @TarunSures41845 @JonSaadFalcon @drmapavone @Azaliamirh @HazyResearch We actually released a robotics version of CLM earlier this year! Check out the CoVer-VLA paper to see how this idea extends to robotics 🤖:
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2103225934338052096/img/SpN3k4PIm34Dp4X_.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/amplify_video/2103225934338052096/vid/avc1/480x270/SOFXZJC8fJBD1Fpp.mp4?tag=29
────────
[4/14] Introducing Contrastive Language Model (CLM): an ultra-fast System One Model trained with a contrastive learning objective that connects states and actions.
CLM-8B is pre-trained on internet-scale data and delivers up to 9× faster inference than Jev ⚡ while achieving comparable performance across computer-use, gaming, and tool-calling tasks.
With lightweight fine-tuning, CLM-8B sets a new SOTA on challenging agentic coding benchmarks, such as DeepSWE (81.6%) and Terminal-Bench 2.1 (87.6%). In contrast, Jev fails to serve as an effective verifier for these long-horizon tasks.
We also build an efficient training and serving infra for CLMs by disaggregating states and actions, allowing their embeddings to be cached and reused independently. This substantially reduces inference latency in settings where the state evolves continuously while the action set remains fixed.
Finally, we establish scaling laws for CLMs and show that the test contrastive loss decreases predictably as a power law in training compute, model size, and dataset size.
📄 Blog:
💻 Code:
🗣️ Discord:
🤗 Data & Models:
More details on CLM’s architecture, data recipe, and scaling laws in the thread below 🧵
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2102904945213358080/img/ar3CkjNREO6ATW-Q.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/amplify_video/2102904945213358080/vid/avc1/480x270/xW0PtwCO0AWYgPUu.mp4?tag=29
────────
[5/14] 🧵(1) Model Architecture
CLM first trains a state encoder and an action encoder on a large-scale dataset with a contrastive objective, so that each state is pulled toward the ground-truth action and pushed away from all others. The two encoders then serve directly as a zero-shot action classifier.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HS8GINibcAEmvkn.jpg
────────
[6/14] 🧵(2) Data Recipe
We release CLM-8B, which is pre-trained on 60M Nemotron Q&A pairs, mid-trained on 30M synthetic hard negatives, and post-trained on 1M agentic trajectories.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HS8GT1HaIAA2tUt.jpg
────────
[7/14] 🧵(3) Scaling Laws for Verification
We find that the test InfoNCE loss scales as a power law with training compute, dataset size, projection-head size, and encoder size. These dimensions must be scaled jointly to achieve optimal performance. Notably, scaling the encoder size yields the strongest gains.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HS8Ge4abQAAfv76.jpg
────────
[8/14] 🧵(4) Latency vs. Jev and Constrained Decoding
The key difference between CLM and Jev is that Jev only supports state caching, whereas CLM’s dual-encoder architecture allows state and action embeddings to be cached independently.
This is particularly useful in applications such as tool calling, computer use, and games, where the action space is predefined and remains fixed.
By caching the action embeddings, CLM substantially reduces inference cost, with the efficiency gains becoming even larger as the number and length of candidate actions grow. At ~1K candidates, CLM is 13× faster than Jev ⚡
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HS8H9_obMAATDnC.jpg
────────
[9/14] 🧵(5) Zero-Shot Evaluation
Across computer-use, gaming, and tool-calling tasks, CLM-8B performs on par with Jev while running up to 9× faster. The speedups are most pronounced when the number of candidates is large (e.g., WikiRacing) or when actions can be reused frequently across states (e.g., T-Rex Game).
CLM-35B, with improved generalization and even greater speedups, will be released early next month.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HS8ImCnbUAAzmkp.png
────────
[10/14] 🧵(6) Agentic Benchmarks
We find that Jev fails to serve as a verifier for long-horizon tasks, performing below the random-selection (Pass@1) baseline.
In contrast, with lightweight fine-tuning, CLM achieves SOTA performance on challenging agentic benchmarks, including DeepSWE (81.6%) and Terminal-Bench 2.1 (87.6%), while delivering 4–6× faster inference than Jev.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HS8JGTsbUAAe8gv.jpg
────────

🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2102910060783628288/img/G5ZKDQ8ECecYtTdg.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/amplify_video/2102910060783628288/vid/avc1/480x270/YJ2CARLBi5nPClRK.mp4?tag=29

clean_summary:
You often need models that quickly decide the right action given a state, like in games or tool use. Traditional models like Jev cache only states, which limits speed when many candidate actions exist or actions repeat often.

CLM trains separate encoders for states and actions with a contrastive objective, letting it cache and reuse embeddings independently. This design makes CLM-8B up to 9× faster than Jev while matching its accuracy on tasks like computer use and gaming. Lightweight fine-tuning boosts CLM to new state-of-the-art results on long-horizon agentic benchmarks. CLM-35B, a larger multimodal version, is coming soon with more data and compute. The team also established scaling laws showing predictable improvements with more compute, data, and model size.
